claims.text: A compositionally complex alloy, specifically a high-entropy alloy, can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The proposed ductile–brittle–ductile behavior results from resistance to temper embrittlement.
The high-entropy alloy is initially in an annealed state.
Temperature-controlled mechanical testing and molecular dynamics simulations can be used to evaluate the hypothesis.
Temper embrittlement occurs in conventional alloys within a narrow temperature window.
Grain-boundary structure mediates the proposed resistance to temper embrittlement.
Elemental segregation at grain boundaries mediates the proposed resistance to temper embrittlement.
The high-entropy alloy has a unique grain-boundary structure and elemental-segregation behavior.
The proposed grain-boundary structure and elemental segregation hinder the formation of brittle phases.
Hindering brittle-phase formation gives the high-entropy alloy resistance to temper embrittlement.
The high-entropy alloy will have 30% greater ductility than conventional alloys within the specified temperature window.
The exact mechanism of temper-embrittlement resistance in high-entropy alloys is not fully understood.
Temper-embrittlement resistance may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions.
A ductility decrease greater than 20% within the narrow temperature window would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis proposes a ductile–brittle–ductile transition, which requires an intervening brittle regime, while the mechanism says brittle-phase formation is hindered and the predicted outcome only specifies enhanced ductility. Thus, the stated mechanism and outcome explain suppression of brittleness rather than the proposed transition through brittleness.
